name: Kinande
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Mutaka, Ngessimo M. 2014. Penultimate lengthening and stress in Kinande. International Journal of Language Studies 8(1): 109-124. (Earlier printing: Mutaka 2000, in F. Remotti (ed.), Environment, languages, cultures, 103-117, Alessandria: Edizioni dell'Orso.) Corroboration: Mutaka, Ngessimo M. 2007. Kinande: A grammar sketch (v1.0), Rutgers African Anaphora Project, p.1; Philippson, Gérard. 1991. Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique Orientale, thèse d'Etat, Paris V, p.483 (sec. 3.5.2, class (c)); Kenstowicz, Michael. 2008. On the origin of tonal classes in Kinande noun stems. Studies in African Linguistics 37(2): 115-151, p.120 + fn.2; Hyman, Larry M. 2009. Penultimate lengthening in Bantu: Analysis and spread. UC Berkeley Phonology Lab Annual Report 2009, table (7) + fn.5 (second-hand).
catalog_quote: [p.110] It should be pointed out that length is not contrastive in Kinande. Therefore, the nouns in (1a) cannot be assigned a long vowel underlyingly. Moreover, penultimate vowel length is predictable in that it always targets the penultimate syllable position of a form within an intonation phrase. [p.112] Since it invariably surfaces on the penultimate syllable nucleus, it is easy to infer that the penultimate syllable is assigned a stress that is manifested by means of vowel lengthening. As will be shown later, penultimate lengthening occurs at the intonational phrase level. ... 5. Penultimate stress: Make a final light syllable of an Intonational Phrase extrametrical. Construct an unbounded right headed domain. ... This rule says: a monomoraic stressed syllable becomes bimoraic. Since the penultimate syllable nucleus is the stress bearing unit, it thus lengthens. [p.121] ... the following data suggest that Kinande stress is assigned at the intonational phrase domain. ... If Penultimate Stress was assigned at the phonological phrase, we would expect ɔtugulu in (17b) to undergo penultimate vowel lengthening. [p.123] In conclusion, it has been argued in this paper that penultimate lengthening is the manifestation of a metrical representation of stress in the intonational phrase prosodic domain. More specifically, it has been argued that a penultimate light syllable becomes heavy at the end of an intonational phrase domain.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Nande (nand1264) is not in the catalog. Two works with stress in the title: (1) Mutaka 1995 (LINCOM chapter on 'prosodic circumscription' of Kinande verbal forms) — no open copy anywhere reachable (no DOI; not on OpenAlex/S2/Crossref/archive.org; from the title and Mutaka's parallel work it is most likely about reduplication/prosodic-morphological domains rather than stress placement; priority low. (2) Philippson 1991 doctoral thesis — theses.fr says not accessible, but the author's DDL lab page links a full open PDF (http://www.ddl.cnrs.fr/Fulltext/philippson/these.pdf), downloaded (542 pp. it types Nande/Konzo as penultimate prominence by length (and intensity) without pitch culmination (p. 484; annex p. 498), notes Nande has neutralised the length opposition (p. 488) and that the penultimate is not a tone attractor (p. 489); Nande data drawn partly from Hyman & Valinande 1985 and Mutaka 1988/1989. Best first-hand statement remains Mutaka 2014 p. 112 (held by the project from the earlier reading; read): penultimate stress realised as penultimate lengthening, assigned at the intonational-phrase level, exceptions only in -aC- verb forms. everything above came from direct downloads and APIs.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kinande is a two-tone (H/L) language; the only stress-like prominence is on the penultimate syllable of the last word of an intonational phrase (which includes words in isolation/citation forms), where it is realised as vowel lengthening; there is no contrastive length. The author analyses this as penultimate stress (final light syllable extrametrical, right-headed unbounded domain, stressed monomoraic syllable becomes bimoraic).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not analysed. Footnote 6 (p.120) says that in Kinande, as in many Narrow Bantu languages, the root vowel is usually considered as bearing a stress (it hosts all vowel contrasts) and suggests the stem might be parsed into two unbounded feet (root vowel + penult); no data on secondary prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: Verb forms containing the tense formative -aC- (imperative, remote past, immediate past, forms in -aya/-awa; historically *-ag-) do not show penultimate length, analysed as a phantom consonant making the syllable already heavy (pp.113-118); demonstratives in -lya (olya, kalya, kirya) lack it and must be lexically marked (p.113 + fn.3); forms uttered with question intonation show no penultimate lengthening (fn.3 p.113; Hyman 2009 table 7: declaratives only, not Y/N or WH questions or ideophones); in a Semliki-plain dialect the formative surfaces as -ag- and does lengthen (p.115).
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly phrase-level: stress/lengthening is assigned at the intonational phrase, not the phonological word or phonological phrase (sec. 4, data (17): a phrase-medial word, even a subject NP forming its own phonological phrase, has no penultimate length). Words in isolation therefore always show it; the phrasal H boundary tone targets the final/penultimate vowel independently of stress. Data are the author's own (native speaker), 'standard Kinande', declarative intonation.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Kinande (Nande) of eastern DRC, the author's native language, referred to as 'standard Kinande'; a Semliki-plain dialect at the foot of the Ruwenzori is mentioned only for the -ag- formative (p.115). Mutaka 2007 p.1 states Kinande 'is basically the same language as Konjo' (Konzo, ISO koo, Uganda), which Glottolog treats separately; the statement is for the DRC Nande variety, glottocode nand1264.

tone_statements.citation: Cho, Hyesun (조혜선). 2013. Effects of tonal distance and speech rate in the phonetic realization of Kinande H tones. Studies in Phonetics, Phonology and Morphology (음성음운형태론연구) 19(3): 501-527. The Phonology-Morphology Circle of Korea.
tone_statements.quote: In Kinande, tones are contrastive in lexical meaning as well as in grammatical function. Kinande has two basic tones (High and Low) and a Falling tone, and the rising tone is very rare (Mutaka 1990, 2007). It is also suggested that Kinande has High, Low, and toneless contrasts underlyingly on the final syllable of disyllabic nouns (Hyman 1990, Kenstowicz 2008). ... Kinande has phrasal H tone and intonational H tone, in addition to lexical H tone (Hyman 1990, Akinlabi and Mutaka 2001, Jones 2010). Phrasal H tone appears usually on the penultimate syllable
tone_statements.locator: p. 503, sec. 1.2 Basic properties of Kinande tones
tone_statements.summary: Count 2 = the 'two basic tones' (H, L); Falling and a rare rising also named. Roots/tense markers H or toneless, other affixes toneless (after Black 1995). Stress only via Mutaka 2014 in fn. 1.

tone_statements.citation: Jones, Patrick. 2011. New evidence for a phonological stem domain in Kinande. In Proceedings of the 28th West Coast Conference on Formal Linguistics (WCCFL 28), 285-293. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla Proceedings Project (paper 2461).
tone_statements.quote: Kinande infinitives, like most words in the language, are always assigned two intonational tones in utterance-final position: H% and L// (Hyman 1990). ... Infinitives whose roots are CVC or larger show the canonical pattern of intonational tone, in which H% is realized on the penult and L// is realized on the ultima (8). ... Verb roots in Kinande fall into two main classes: tonic roots, which contribute an underlying H tone to the verb stem in which they appear, and non-tonic roots, which do not.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2.1, p. 287 and sec. 2.2 opening, p. 289
tone_statements.summary: Lexical H vs zero on verb roots (tonic/non-tonic) plus boundary tones H%, L//; falling tones derived (H%+L// on one vowel, or L epenthesis); no tone count; TBU = vowel or glide; L// = L, subscript //.

tone_statements.citation: Kenstowicz, Michael. 2008. On the origin of tonal classes in Kinande noun stems. Studies in African Linguistics 37(2): 115-151. doi:10.32473/sal.v37i2.107295.
tone_statements.quote: In one of the first investigations of the tonology of the Bantu language Kinande (D42), Hyman (1990) isolated the six contrasting tone patterns of (1a) for disyllabic noun stems. They arise principally from a process shifting a high tone (H) one syllable to the left. ... Words like e-ki-tsungu and e-kí-koba that block the attachment of the H-L% are assigned an underlying final low tone (L). ... Kinande thus presents an underlying ternary /H-L-0/ contrast on the final syllable of disyllabic stems in this analysis.
tone_statements.summary: Lexical H vs L vs toneless on noun stems (six classes /00 0L H0 HL 0H HH/), leftward H shift, phrasal H-L% boundary tones; floating H for one class (p. 132); downstep only as a historical guess.

tone_statements.quote: In Kinande, the penultimate vowel is usually lengthened before a pause (see the examples in (a) below). There are very few exceptions as in (b) These end in the historical -ag- and that Mutaka (1994) analyses as -aC- where C is a phantom consonant [...] We completely ignore this penultimate lengthening in this dictionary. | Notice also that there is usually a H tone on the penultimate vowel. This H is phrasal. If the word is followed by something else, this phrasal H does not show up | this phrasal H always targets the penultimate vowel either of the word, and if the verb form is part of a phrase, here verb + object, this H surfaces on the penultimate vowel of the last word in the phrase, (here on Magulu). | It should be observed that whereas the phrasal H targets the underlying penultimate vowel, penultimate lengthening, that is the lengthening of the penultimate vowel, targets the phonetic vowel of the penultimate syllable.

tone_statements.citation: Akinlabí, Akinbiyi M. and Mutaka, Ngessimo M. (2001). Tone in the infinitive in Kinande: an OT analysis. In Research mate in African linguistics: Focus on Cameroon. Köln: Rüdiger Köppe, pp. 333-356.
tone_statements.quote: Following Hyman (1990), we assume that the H on the penultimate vowel in (5a) is a phrasal tone and the L on the final vowel (unmarked here) is an intonational tone. This is made obvious in (5b) where we have added a name after the verb. What happens is that the phrasal H now surfaces on the penultimate vowel of the entire utterance and the intonational L surfaces on its final vowel. [p. 336] ... So far, we have postulated the following tones: (i) Phrasal H tone (ii) List intonation H tone (iii) Utterance final L tone. The phrasal H may appear on the final vowel or on the penultimate vowel whereas the intonational tone (H or L) appears on the final vowel. [p. 337] ... Of interest here is the lexical H tone of the verb root which anticipates once onto the preceding vowel in forms without an object marker (8a, 9a), and twice in forms with the object marker (8b, 9b). This lexical H never surfaces on its underlying tone bearing unit, that is, on the root vowel. [p. 338]

tone_statements.summary: Tone only: lexical H vs toneless verb roots (-tum- vs -hum-), a phrasal H (after Hyman 1990) on the final vowel of a phonological phrase (verb in subject position, e.g. erihume siryowe:ne 'to hit is not good') or on the penult when an intonational boundary tone (utterance-final L, or list-intonation H) takes the final vowel; verb-root lexical H is realized on the INFL-final vowel (-ri-/-na-), neve

tone_statements.citation: Mutaka, Ngessimo M. (1995). Vowel harmony in Kinande. Journal of West African Languages 25. pp. 42-55.
tone_statements.quote: The high tone is represented by an acute accent, the low tone is unmarked, the phrasal H is also unmarked when it appears on the penultimate vowel. A falling tone on the final vowel is marked by a caret. Such a falling tone is the result of a phrasal H on the penultimate vowel and a default L tone on the final vowel as in tu-ka-hum-a-a [tukaehuma] 'we are hitting' [scanned: diacritics on the example garbled]. Also, a low tone is marked with a grave accent in words whose penultimate vowel does not surface with a phrasal H as in mo-twaswere 'we ground'.

sources.quote: In Kinande, tones are contrastive in lexical meaning as well as in grammatical function. Kinande has two basic tones (High and Low) and a Falling tone, and the rising tone is very rare (Mutaka 1990, 2007). sources.quote: Kinande infinitives, like most words in the language, are always assigned two intonational tones in utterance-final position: H% and L// (Hyman 1990). ... Infinitives whose roots are CVC or larger show the canonical pattern of intonational tone, in which H% is realized on the penult and L// is realized on the ultima (8). ... Verb roots in Kinande fall into two main classes: tonic roots, which contribute an underlying H tone to the verb stem in which they appear, and non-tonic roots, which do not.

sources.quote: In one of the first investigations of the tonology of the Bantu language Kinande (D42), Hyman (1990) isolated the six contrasting tone patterns of (1a) for disyllabic noun stems. They arise principally from a process shifting a high tone (H) one syllable to the left. ... Words like e-ki-tsungu and e-kí-koba that block the attachment of the H-L% are assigned an underlying final low tone (L). ... Kinande thus presents an underlying ternary /H-L-0/ contrast on the final syllable of disyllabic stems in this analysis.
sources.note: Lexical H vs L vs toneless on noun stems (six classes /00 0L H0 HL 0H HH/), leftward H shift, phrasal H-L% boundary tones; floating H for one class (p. 132); downstep only as a historical guess.

sources.quote: Following Hyman (1990), we assume that the H on the penultimate vowel in (5a) is a phrasal tone and the L on the final vowel (unmarked here) is an intonational tone. This is made obvious in (5b) where we have added a name after the verb. What happens is that the phrasal H now surfaces on the penultimate vowel of the entire utterance and the intonational L surfaces on its final vowel. [p. 336] ... So far, we have postulated the following tones: (i) Phrasal H tone (ii) List intonation H tone (iii) Utterance final L tone. The phrasal H may appear on the final vowel or on the penultimate vowel whereas the intonational tone (H or L) appears on the final vowel. [p. 337] ... Of interest here is the lexical H tone of the verb root which anticipates once onto the preceding vowel in forms without an object marker (8a, 9a), and twice in forms with the object marker (8b, 9b). This lexical H never surfaces on its underlying tone bearing unit, that is, on the root vowel. [p. 338]

sources.quote: The high tone is represented by an acute accent, the low tone is unmarked, the phrasal H is also unmarked when it appears on the penultimate vowel. A falling tone on the final vowel is marked by a caret. Such a falling tone is the result of a phrasal H on the penultimate vowel and a default L tone on the final vowel as in tu-ka-hum-a-a [tukaehuma] 'we are hitting' [scanned: diacritics on the example garbled]. Also, a low tone is marked with a grave accent in words whose penultimate vowel does not surface with a phrasal H as in mo-twaswere 'we ground'.

sources.note: Vowel-harmony paper; tone appears only in a transcription-conventions footnote and passing remarks. States lexical H vs L tone, a phrasal H on the penultimate vowel (with a default L giving a final falling tone), and penultimate length as a postlexical rule alongside the phrasal H (abbreviation PL = penultimate length, p. 44 n. 6). No word 'stress' anywhere. Consistent with the catalog's phrasal kind and tone-and-stress class for nand1264 (Mutaka 2014 penultimate lengthening). Suffixal-H facts are cited to Mutaka (1990).
